title: The Art of War
author: Sun Tzu
summary:
The Art of War is a classical Chinese military treatise traditionally attributed to a strategist named Sun Wu, better known by the honorific Sun Tzu (Master Sun), who later Chinese historians place in the state of Wu around the 6th century BCE. Exactly who composed the text, and when, is a genuinely open question among historians — a subject this entry's Author tab addresses directly — but the work itself is remarkably consistent in its argument: war is not primarily a contest of courage or numbers, but a discipline of positioning, timing, and information, and the highest form of victory is one that subdues an opponent without a battle ever being fought.

The text's opening move is to insist that war is too consequential to enter without exhaustive prior calculation. Before any campaign, a commander should weigh five constant factors — moral cohesion between ruler and people, the conditions of weather and season, the realities of terrain, the quality of command, and the discipline of method — and compare his own position against the enemy's across seven concrete measures. Woven through this calculation is a second, complementary principle: deception. All warfare, the text insists, is based on appearing where you are not expected, seeming weak when strong and strong when weak, and shaping what an opponent believes about you long before any engagement begins.

Much of the text translates this preparation into action by exploiting imbalance. A skilled commander stays formless and unpredictable, forcing an opponent to guard every position and therefore be strong nowhere in particular, while concentrating his own strength at the single point that matters. Tactics should flow like water, avoiding what is strong and striking what is weak, adapting constantly to terrain and circumstance rather than repeating a plan that worked once. The text catalogues specific types of ground — accessible, entangling, narrow passes, desperate — each demanding a different posture, and warns that most military disasters trace back not to bad terrain or a strong enemy but to a commander's own failures of calculation, authority, or discipline.

Leadership runs through the text as both a practical and a moral concern. A general needs wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage, and strictness in combination, and must guard against five specific character flaws — recklessness, cowardice, a quick temper, an excessive sense of honor, and over-concern for his men — any one of which an opponent can exploit. The text is emphatic that prolonged war benefits no one, since even a mediocre quick resolution outperforms a brilliant, drawn-out one, and it insists that no ruler or general should ever commit to conflict out of anger or wounded pride, since only calculated advantage justifies the cost. The closing chapter argues that foreknowledge — gained above all through espionage — is the single most valuable resource available to a commander, cheap in comparison to the alternative of fighting blind.

Written roughly 2,500 years ago for a world of chariots and rival feudal states, the text's continued relevance far outside military contexts — in business strategy, negotiation, sport, and law — comes from treating any sustained competitive situation as fundamentally a matter of information, positioning, timing, and the discipline to avoid a costly confrontation whenever a better path exists.

sections.title: Laying Plans
sections.summary:
Laying Plans opens the text with its foundational claim: war is a matter of life and death for the state, and no ruler or general has the right to enter into it without first working through a rigorous set of calculations. Before any campaign begins, the chapter insists, victory or defeat can already be forecast by comparing the two sides across a fixed set of factors — not through guesswork or divination, but through disciplined analysis of exactly what each side actually has.

The chapter lays out five constant factors that determine a state's military condition — moral cohesion between ruler and people, the conditions of heaven (weather, timing, season), the realities of earth (terrain, distance, danger), the quality of the commander, and the discipline of method and organization — and translates them into seven direct comparisons a strategist can make between two rival forces: which ruler commands more loyalty, which general is more capable, which side holds the advantages of terrain and season, whose discipline is more rigorously enforced, whose army is stronger, whose troops are better trained, and whose system of reward and punishment is more consistent. Whichever side scores better across these measures, the chapter argues, can already be identified as the likely winner before a single battle is fought.

The chapter's final movement turns from calculation to concealment: having worked out the true state of affairs, a commander must actively hide it. All warfare is based on deception — seeming unable when able, inactive when active, far when near, weak when strong — and using every device available to make an opponent's expectations diverge from reality. The chapter closes by tying the two themes together: the side that makes the most calculations beforehand, in the privacy of the command tent, is the side most likely to win, and the side that makes none is all but guaranteed to lose.
keyLessons: Work through a fixed set of factors — leadership, timing, terrain, discipline, morale — before committing to any high-stakes contest, rather than trusting instinct alone.
Compare your own position against a rival's across concrete measures, not vague impressions, to forecast who actually has the advantage.
Build deception into a plan from the start; making an opponent's expectations wrong is as valuable as any single tactical move.

sections.title: Waging War
sections.summary:
Waging War shifts from planning to cost, opening with a specific accounting of what fielding a large army actually requires — chariots, armor, provisions, and a daily expenditure the chapter puts at a thousand ounces of silver for a hundred-thousand-man force. The purpose of these numbers is not bookkeeping for its own sake; it is to establish, in concrete terms, exactly how much a state stands to lose for every day a war continues.

From that foundation the chapter builds its central warning: no country has ever benefited from a long war. Weapons grow dull, enthusiasm fades, treasuries empty, and — most dangerously — a state weakened by protracted conflict invites opportunistic rivals to strike while its guard is down. The chapter's well-known position is that stupid haste has at least sometimes worked in war, but that clever, drawn-out campaigns never have; speed, even at the cost of elegance, beats brilliance stretched over time. Practically, the chapter recommends provisioning an army from the enemy's own territory rather than hauling supplies from home, on the logic that a single cartload of captured provisions is worth twenty hauled from a distance.

The chapter closes on a point about converting captured strength into your own: soldiers should be rewarded for what they capture, and captured chariots and men should be absorbed and used rather than merely destroyed, turning a defeated enemy into an addition to your own force. Its final line makes the stakes explicit — the general who leads an army is the arbiter of the people's fate, the person on whom the whole nation's peace or peril actually depends.
keyLessons: Know the real, concrete cost of sustaining a long conflict before committing to one — the numbers usually argue for speed over elegance.
A country that wins slowly still loses; there is no recorded case of a state benefiting from a prolonged war.
Convert captured resources and personnel into your own strength wherever possible, rather than only depleting the enemy.

sections.title: Attack by Stratagem
sections.summary:
Attack by Stratagem introduces the text's most famous idea: that supreme excellence in war is not winning every battle you fight, but breaking an opponent's resistance without ever having to fight at all. The chapter opens by valuing an intact victory — capturing a country, an army, or a city whole — above a destructive one, since a shattered prize is worth less than a preserved one.

From there the chapter ranks strategies from best to worst: the highest form of generalship is to frustrate an enemy's plans before they can be executed; next best is to prevent an enemy's alliances from forming; next is to attack the enemy's army directly in the field; and the worst option of all, to be avoided whenever possible, is besieging a walled city, a slow and costly last resort. The chapter then sets out practical rules for matching force to the situation — surrounding an equal-strength enemy is different from attacking when outnumbering him five to one, dividing forces when twice as strong, and knowing when to offer battle, avoid it, or simply flee.

The chapter's second half turns to the relationship between ruler and general, warning that a sovereign can bring disaster on his own army by commanding movements the army cannot execute, by governing military affairs the way he governs civil ones, or by interfering with command decisions out of ignorance of conditions in the field. It closes with the text's single most quoted line: know the enemy and know yourself, and a hundred battles need not be feared; know yourself alone, and victory and defeat will split evenly; know neither, and every battle will end in defeat.
keyLessons: Rank your options: frustrating an opponent's plans beats breaking alliances, which beats direct confrontation, which beats a prolonged siege — work down that list in order.
Match your posture to the real force ratio in front of you rather than applying one fixed approach regardless of relative strength.
Self-knowledge and knowledge of the opponent are equally necessary; missing either one caps your odds at fifty-fifty, and missing both guarantees loss.

sections.title: Tactical Dispositions
sections.summary:
Tactical Dispositions turns from strategy to the concrete arrangement of forces, opening with a distinction the rest of the chapter builds on: securing yourself against defeat is entirely within your own control, but actually defeating the enemy depends on the enemy giving you an opening. A skilled commander, the chapter argues, makes himself unbeatable first and only then watches for a genuine opportunity to win — rather than gambling an unsecured position for a chance at victory.

This produces one of the text's most striking claims: the truly skilled fighter's victories bring him no reputation for wisdom and no credit for courage, because the battle was effectively won before it was fought, and to the outside world it can look almost effortless — lifting something already light, not something heavy. What looks to the crowd like a difficult, hard-won triumph is, to Sun Tzu, actually a lesser achievement than a victory secured so thoroughly in advance that it never looked dramatic at all.

The chapter closes by laying out a chain of reasoning that runs from measurement of terrain to estimation of relative quantity to calculation to a weighing of chances to victory itself — each step depending on the one before it, so that skipping a step just relocates the guesswork rather than eliminating it. A victorious army facing a defeated one, the chapter concludes, is like a heavy weight dropped against a light one: not a close contest at all, but the visible result of an imbalance created well before the fighting started.
keyLessons: Make your own position unbeatable first; only then look for a genuine opportunity to beat the opponent, rather than risking your foundation for a chance at victory.
The clearest, best-prepared victories often look effortless and draw little credit — don't mistake a hard-fought win for a well-prepared one.
Work through the full chain from measurement to calculation to victory in order; shortcuts just move the uncertainty to a later, more costly point.

sections.title: Energy
sections.summary:
Energy explores how a commander generates decisive force without simply outnumbering an opponent. Its central technical distinction is between direct methods (used to engage an enemy head-on) and indirect methods (used to secure the actual victory) — the two working together, the chapter argues, in combinations as inexhaustible as the flow of rivers or the changing of the seasons, even though only a handful of underlying elements are ever in play.

The chapter builds toward two vivid images for how this energy should feel in practice: decision should strike like a falcon's well-timed swoop, and accumulated force should move like a round stone rolled down a mountain, gathering unstoppable momentum from terrain and shape rather than from constant individual effort. A skilled commander, the chapter argues, looks to the effect of combined energy rather than demanding perfection from every individual soldier — placing the right people correctly matters more than expecting excellence from everyone.

The chapter's closing movement addresses appearances: simulated disorder requires real underlying discipline to pull off convincingly, simulated fear requires real courage, and simulated weakness requires real strength — deception of this kind is not the absence of the true quality but a controlled performance built on top of it. A skilled commander uses this to keep an opponent moving and off-balance, holding out bait to lure him and picked troops in reserve to spring on him once he takes it.
keyLessons: Combine direct, expected moves with indirect, surprising ones; the possible combinations from a small set of tools are genuinely inexhaustible.
Build momentum deliberately, the way a stone gathers speed rolling downhill, rather than relying on sustained individual exertion.
Convincing displays of disorder, fear, or weakness require real discipline, courage, or strength underneath them — deception is a controlled performance, not an absence of substance.

sections.title: Weak Points and Strong
sections.summary:
Weak Points and Strong opens with a simple asymmetry: whoever occupies the field first and waits is fresh for the fight, while whoever arrives second, rushing to catch up, arrives exhausted. From this the chapter builds its central argument — a skilled commander imposes his own will on the enemy's movements rather than reacting to the enemy's, using bait, harassment, and pressure to make the opponent go where the commander wants rather than the other way around.

The chapter's key technical idea is formlessness: by concealing your own dispositions while discovering the enemy's, you force him to prepare against attack at many possible points at once, thinning his strength everywhere, while your own force stays concentrated and can strike any single point with overwhelming relative numbers. Attack only where the enemy is undefended, the chapter argues, and defend only positions that cannot be attacked — an aphorism the chapter itself calls the whole art of war compressed into a single principle.

The chapter closes with its famous water metaphor: just as water has no constant shape and always flows from high ground to low, a skilled commander has no fixed method and always moves from the enemy's strength toward the enemy's weakness. Because conditions never repeat exactly, the chapter warns against reusing a tactic that won once before; the commander who can continually reshape his approach to the specific opponent in front of him, the way water reshapes itself to any container, deserves to be called heaven-born.
keyLessons: Force the enemy to react to your movements rather than reacting to his; dictating terms matters more than raw strength.
Stay formless and unpredictable so the enemy must guard everywhere and is therefore strong nowhere in particular, while you concentrate your own force at the point that matters.
Never repeat a winning tactic mechanically — conditions change, and a method that worked once can fail the next time exactly because the enemy now expects it.

sections.title: Maneuvering
sections.summary:
Maneuvering addresses one of the text's hardest practical problems: how to turn a roundabout, disadvantageous route into one that actually beats a rival to the objective. The chapter opens by naming this the artifice of deviation — enticing an opponent off the direct path, or accepting a longer route yourself, in exchange for arriving in a stronger position or ahead of schedule despite the detour.

Much of the chapter is a practical warning about the risks of speed itself: forced marches that cover too much ground too quickly exhaust an army and can strand its strongest and weakest elements far apart, so that a march pushed too hard for a quick advantage can cost a general his leading officers and the bulk of his force before a single battle is fought. The chapter's instruction for the right pace under different conditions became one of its most quoted passages: move with the speed of wind, hold formation like a forest, consume like fire when raiding, stay immovable as a mountain when holding ground, and strike, when the moment comes, like a thunderbolt.

The chapter closes with observations on morale and restraint: a soldier's spirit is sharpest in the morning and fades by evening, so a wise commander avoids an enemy at its most spirited and strikes when it is flagging; and an enemy that is truly desperate, with no possible retreat, should never be pressed too hard, since a surrounded force with nothing left to lose will fight far harder than one given a visible way out.
keyLessons: Turning a longer or harder route into the faster path — through misdirection, patience, or better use of terrain — is the core skill of effective maneuvering.
Match your posture to the moment: swift as wind on the move, disciplined as a forest in formation, consuming as fire when attacking, immovable as a mountain when holding.
Always leave a desperate opponent some way out; a force with nothing left to lose will fight far harder than a force you allow to retreat.

sections.title: Variation of Tactics
sections.summary:
Variation of Tactics is the text's shortest chapter and its most direct statement that rules of thumb are only a starting point. It opens by listing situations calling for departures from standard practice — certain kinds of ground should not be camped on, certain roads not followed, certain positions not contested, and, most strikingly, certain commands from the ruler himself not obeyed, if obeying them would lose the battle.

The chapter's core argument is that knowing the general advantages of a situation is worthless without also weighing the disadvantages folded into it, and vice versa — a wise commander blends both into every plan, since one-sided thinking about only the upside or only the risk produces fragile decisions. A general who knows the textbook advantages but can't vary his plans to fit the actual moment in front of him, the chapter warns, will still fail to get the best use out of his own men.

The chapter closes with a list of five dangerous character flaws in a commander that an alert opponent can exploit: recklessness, which leads to destruction; cowardice, which leads to capture; a quick temper, which can be provoked by insults into a bad decision; an excessive sense of personal honor, which is vulnerable to calculated shame; and over-concern for his own men's comfort, which exposes him to constant worry and can override sound judgment. The chapter states plainly that when an army is overthrown and its leader killed, the cause is almost always traceable to one of these five faults.
keyLessons: Treat standard rules and doctrine as a starting point, not a substitute for judgment about the specific, changing situation in front of you.
Weigh the disadvantage folded into every apparent advantage, and the advantage folded into every apparent disadvantage — one-sided thinking produces fragile plans.
Watch for the five character flaws — recklessness, cowardice, a quick temper, an inflated sense of honor, over-concern for comfort — that let an opponent manipulate a commander, including yourself.

sections.title: The Army on the March
sections.summary:
The Army on the March shifts from strategic principle to field craft, opening with practical guidance for encamping and moving through four kinds of terrain — mountains, rivers, marshes, and flat country — each requiring a different posture, but all governed by a shared preference for high, dry, sunny ground over low, damp, shaded ground, both for tactical advantage and for the health of the troops.

The chapter's longest and most distinctive section catalogues how to read an enemy's true condition from small, indirect signals rather than direct communication: dust rising high signals chariots, low and spread-out dust signals infantry; birds startling into flight reveal a hidden ambush; soldiers leaning on their spears are faint from hunger; men whispering in small groups signal disaffection in the ranks; and an army that kills its draft animals for food and abandons its own cooking-pots has committed to fighting to the death rather than returning to camp. Read together, the chapter argues, these small physical details reveal an army's real state of morale and intention far more reliably than anything it says.

The chapter closes on discipline, arguing that soldiers punished before they've grown attached to their commander will resist control, while soldiers never held to real discipline once that attachment forms will be equally useless — the two must be built together, humane treatment paired with genuinely enforced standards, producing what the chapter calls a certain road to victory.
keyLessons: Learn to read small, indirect physical signals — dust patterns, animal behavior, whispered conversation, unusual quiet — as reliable evidence of an opponent's real condition and intent.
Match your position and posture to the actual terrain you're in (mountain, river, marsh, plain) rather than applying one fixed approach everywhere.
Build genuine care for your people and real enforced discipline together; either one without the other produces an unreliable force.

sections.title: Terrain
sections.summary:
Terrain catalogues six types of ground — accessible, entangling, temporizing, narrow passes, precipitous heights, and ground far from the enemy — and the specific tactic suited to each, extending the practical, terrain-first thinking of the previous chapter into a fuller system a commander is expected to master before taking a responsible command.

The chapter's real center of gravity, though, is a separate list: six ways an army defeats itself that have nothing to do with terrain or the enemy's strength and everything to do with the general's own failures — flight from being badly outnumbered, insubordination from weak officers over strong troops, collapse from the reverse imbalance, ruin from angry subordinate officers engaging without orders, disorganization from unclear commands, and rout from committing an unprepared or ill-matched force. The chapter is explicit that all six trace back to the commander, not to bad luck or superior terrain, framing most military disaster as a leadership failure in disguise.

The chapter closes on the relationship between duty and obedience: a general who will fight even against the ruler's orders when fighting will win, and who will refuse to fight even at the ruler's insistence when fighting will lose, is called the jewel of the kingdom — not because of ordinary loyalty, but because of a rarer loyalty to the actual mission over the chain of command. The chapter pairs this with a warning against pure indulgence: a commander who treats his soldiers with real care, the way a father treats children, earns their willingness to follow him anywhere, but a commander who is kind without also being able to enforce authority produces spoiled, useless troops.
keyLessons: Match tactics to the specific type of terrain you're actually in — accessible, entangling, narrow, precipitous, distant — rather than a generic approach.
Treat most military disaster as a leadership failure first: nearly every way an army defeats itself traces back to the general's own miscalculation, weak authority, or poor discipline.
Care for your people genuinely, but never let that care become an inability to enforce real standards — indulgence without authority produces an unreliable force.

sections.title: The Nine Situations
sections.summary:
The Nine Situations is the text's longest chapter, extending the terrain analysis of the previous two chapters into nine distinct strategic circumstances an army can find itself in — from dispersive ground fought on home territory, through contested and open ground, to the most extreme category, desperate ground, where an army can only survive by fighting immediately because there is no possibility of retreat.

The chapter's most striking argument is that extreme pressure can produce extreme unity: on desperate ground, the chapter claims, soldiers who might otherwise flee will instead fight with everything they have, because the option of running has been removed. It illustrates the deeper point with a well-known image — a genuinely unified army should respond the way the legendary shuai-jan serpent does, striking back with its tail if struck at the head and with its head if struck at the tail — and the chapter extends the image further: even natural enemies, like the rival peoples of Wu and Yüeh, will help each other without hesitation if caught in the same boat during a storm, because shared, immediate danger overrides ordinary rivalry.

The chapter closes by returning the responsibility for producing that unity to the general himself: it is command — psychological leadership specific to each type of ground, keeping an army ignorant of dangers that would demoralize it, and sometimes deliberately narrowing an army's options — that turns raw troops into a single cohesive body, not the terrain or the danger alone. Nine different kinds of ground call for nine different kinds of leadership response, and mismatching the two undoes whatever advantage the position itself offered.
keyLessons: Extreme circumstances can produce extreme unity — sometimes deliberately narrowing an option (like retreat) sharpens resolve rather than weakening it.
A genuinely unified team responds to a threat the way a single body does, each part reinforcing the others automatically, the way even rivals cooperate against a shared, immediate danger.
Match your leadership approach to the specific psychological state a given situation produces in your people, rather than applying one generic style of encouragement everywhere.

sections.title: The Attack by Fire
sections.summary:
The Attack by Fire opens as a technical manual for one specific weapon, cataloguing five targets for a fire attack — soldiers in camp, stores, baggage trains, arsenals, and the enemy's supply lines — along with the seasonal and astronomical conditions (dry weather, specific lunar positions associated with rising wind) needed to make the tactic work, and five follow-up responses depending on how the fire actually develops.

Partway through, the chapter pivots from the mechanics of fire to a much broader argument about restraint: a ruler should never put troops into the field merely to satisfy his own anger, and a general should never fight a battle out of personal pique, because anger and vexation can pass and be replaced by calm, but a destroyed kingdom can never be restored and the dead can never be brought back to life. The chapter draws a sharp line between reversible costs, which can eventually be recovered from, and irreversible ones, which cannot — and insists that only calculated advantage, never wounded pride, justifies crossing that line.

The chapter closes by tying its opening technical subject back to this larger caution: hence the enlightened ruler is heedful and the good general full of caution, and that combination of capability with restraint, not aggression alone, is what keeps a country at peace and an army intact.
keyLessons: Match specific methods to the specific conditions actually available (season, wind, terrain) rather than forcing a tactic that isn't ready to work.
Never commit forces or start a conflict merely to satisfy anger or wounded pride — only calculated advantage justifies the cost of action.
Distinguish reversible costs from irreversible ones; a destroyed state or a lost life cannot be undone the way a delayed campaign or a spent treasury eventually can.

sections.title: The Use of Spies
sections.summary:
The Use of Spies closes the text by returning to its opening concern — the enormous cost of war — and drawing from it an argument for the value of information. Raising and marching a large army for years, the chapter notes, drains a state's resources and disrupts hundreds of thousands of households; begrudging a comparatively trivial expense to properly pay for intelligence, while a war of that scale drags on in ignorance of the enemy's true condition, the chapter calls nothing less than a failure of basic humanity toward one's own people.

The chapter argues that this crucial foreknowledge cannot come from omens, from reasoning by analogy to past cases, or from abstract calculation — it can only come from other people, and specifically from five distinct categories of spy: local spies drawn from an area's inhabitants, inward spies recruited from the enemy's own officials, converted spies turned from the enemy's own intelligence network, doomed spies deliberately fed false information to carry to the enemy, and surviving spies who simply return alive with what they observed. Working together and kept secret from one another, the chapter argues, these five types form a system so effective it deserves to be called divine.

The chapter closes with practical guidance on managing this system: no one in the army should be treated with more intimacy or rewarded more liberally than spies, and no other area of operations demands greater secrecy, since a leaked secret costs both the spy and whoever heard it their life. Foreknowledge, the chapter concludes, is what let history's most successful rulers achieve results beyond the reach of ordinary men, and because an army's ability to move safely depends on it, spies are among the most important assets available to any commander.
keyLessons: Foreknowledge is worth paying for; the cost of good intelligence is trivial compared to the cost of fighting a prolonged conflict without it.
Different kinds of informants serve different specific purposes — match the type of source to the type of information you actually need.
Trust, reward, and protect the people gathering your information generously and keep their work strictly confidential, or the whole system collapses.
Prepare and position so thoroughly beforehand that the actual confrontation becomes close to a formality — the goal is to win before fighting.
Know yourself and your opponent equally well; most strategic failure comes from an information gap on one side or the other.
Avoid prolonged conflicts — even an imperfect quick resolution usually beats a drawn-out, resource-draining victory.
Attack where an opponent is weak or unprepared, and avoid direct confrontation with their strength.
Stay adaptable; rigid adherence to a fixed plan is a liability once circumstances change.
Secure your own position against failure first, then look for genuine opportunities to win — don't gamble your foundation for a chance at victory.
Never let anger or wounded pride drive a decision; act only on calculated advantage.
Invest in good information (in Sun Tzu's terms, espionage) — it's consistently one of the highest-leverage resources available.
Treat the people who depend on you with genuine care, balanced by real, enforced discipline — either alone produces an unreliable team.

quotes.text: All warfare is based on deception.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. I "Laying Plans" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Attack him where he is unprepared, appear where you are not expected.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. I "Laying Plans" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Hold out baits to entice the enemy. Feign disorder, and crush him.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. I "Laying Plans" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Simulated disorder postulates perfect discipline; simulated fear postulates courage; simulated weakness postulates strength.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. V "Energy" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: All men can see the tactics whereby I conquer, but what none can see is the strategy out of which victory is evolved.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. VI "Weak Points and Strong" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. III "Attack by Stratagem" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)
quotes.category: Winning Without Fighting & the Cost of War

quotes.text: Thus the highest form of generalship is to baulk the enemy's plans; the next best is to prevent the junction of the enemy's forces; the next in order is to attack the enemy's army in the field; and the worst policy of all is to besiege walled cities.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. III "Attack by Stratagem" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)
quotes.category: Winning Without Fighting & the Cost of War

quotes.text: In war, then, let your great object be victory, not lengthy campaigns.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. II "Waging War" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)
quotes.category: Winning Without Fighting & the Cost of War

quotes.text: There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. II "Waging War" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)
quotes.category: Winning Without Fighting & the Cost of War

quotes.text: Thus it may be known that the leader of armies is the arbiter of the people's fate, the man on whom it depends whether the nation shall be in peace or in peril.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. II "Waging War" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)
quotes.category: Winning Without Fighting & the Cost of War

quotes.text: If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat. If you know neither the enemy nor yourself, you will succumb in every battle.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. III "Attack by Stratagem" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. IV "Tactical Dispositions" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: To secure ourselves against defeat lies in our own hands, but the opportunity of defeating the enemy is provided by the enemy himself.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. IV "Tactical Dispositions" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Thus it is that in war the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won, whereas he who is destined to defeat first fights and afterwards looks for victory.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. IV "Tactical Dispositions" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: If you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not stand in doubt; if you know Heaven and know Earth, you may make your victory complete.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. X "Terrain" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Appear at points which the enemy must hasten to defend; march swiftly to places where you are not expected.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. VI "Weak Points and Strong" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Military tactics are like unto water; for water in its natural course runs away from high places and hastens downwards. So in war, the way is to avoid what is strong and to strike at what is weak.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. VI "Weak Points and Strong" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Let your rapidity be that of the wind, your compactness that of the forest. In raiding and plundering be like fire, in immovability like a mountain.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. VII "Maneuvering" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Whoever is first in the field and awaits the coming of the enemy, will be fresh for the fight; whoever is second in the field and has to hasten to battle, will arrive exhausted.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. VI "Weak Points and Strong" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: For the men of Wu and the men of Yüeh are enemies; yet if they are crossing a river in the same boat and are caught by a storm, they will come to each other's assistance just as the left hand helps the right.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. XI "The Nine Situations" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: There are five dangerous faults which may affect a general: (1) Recklessness, which leads to destruction; (2) cowardice, which leads to capture; (3) a hasty temper, which can be provoked by insults; (4) a delicacy of honour which is sensitive to shame; (5) over-solicitude for his men, which exposes him to worry and trouble.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. VIII "Variation of Tactics" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Regard your soldiers as your children, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys; look on them as your own beloved sons, and they will stand by you even unto death.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. X "Terrain" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Therefore soldiers must be treated in the first instance with humanity, but kept under control by means of iron discipline. This is a certain road to victory.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. IX "The Army on the March" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only thought is to protect his country and do good service for his sovereign, is the jewel of the kingdom.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. X "Terrain" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: When you surround an army, leave an outlet free. Do not press a desperate foe too hard.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. VII "Maneuvering" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Thus, what enables the wise sovereign and the good general to strike and conquer, and achieve things beyond the reach of ordinary men, is foreknowledge.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. XIII "The Use of Spies" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Be subtle! be subtle! and use your spies for every kind of business.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. XIII "The Use of Spies" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: No ruler should put troops into the field merely to gratify his own spleen; no general should fight a battle simply out of pique.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. XII "The Attack by Fire" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Anger may in time change to gladness; vexation may be succeeded by content. But a kingdom that has once been destroyed can never come again into being; nor can the dead ever be brought back to life.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. XII "The Attack by Fire" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

quotes.text: Hence the saying: The enlightened ruler lays his plans well ahead; the good general cultivates his resources.
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Ch. XII "The Attack by Fire" (trans. Lionel Giles, 1910)

authorBio.name: Sun Tzu (Sun Wu)
authorBio.bio:
Whether Sun Tzu existed as a single historical individual is a genuinely open question in Chinese studies, not a settled fact papered over by tradition. The traditional account, set down by the Han-dynasty historian Sima Qian in his Records of the Grand Historian roughly two centuries after the events it describes, holds that Sun Wu was a general from the state of Qi who entered the service of King Helü of Wu around the 6th century BCE, proved his discipline by drilling the king's palace concubines into soldiers (executing the two who laughed at his orders), and went on to help Wu defeat the much larger state of Chu at the decisive Battle of Boju in 506 BCE. This is the version most popular accounts still repeat, and it is the reason Sun Tzu is often dated to roughly 544-496 BCE.

The case against taking this account at face value is substantial. The Zuo Zhuan, a detailed and far more contemporary history of the same Wu-Chu wars, describes the Battle of Boju at length but never once mentions Sun Wu — a silence historians have found difficult to explain if he had really commanded a campaign of that scale. Scholars as far back as the Song dynasty (and Lionel Giles himself, in his 1910 translator's introduction, which questioned the concubine-drill story as "utterly preposterous and incredible") have also pointed to anachronisms in the text itself — references to crossbows, cavalry, and forms of military organization that historians generally place later, in the Warring States period — suggesting the surviving Art of War may not have reached its current form until well after Sun Wu's supposed lifetime, if he existed at all.

Out of this, two broad scholarly positions have emerged, and neither has won a decisive victory over the other. One holds that a real strategist named Sun Wu did serve Wu roughly as described, and that the text's apparent anachronisms reflect later editing of an authentic core rather than wholesale invention. The other holds that Sun Tzu functioned more as a title or a legendary figurehead — Master Sun — under whose name a body of military thought, possibly compiled by more than one hand over generations, was gathered and credited. A 1972 archaeological discovery at Yinqueshan in Shandong complicated the picture further rather than resolving it: excavators found Han-dynasty bamboo-strip copies of both the Art of War attributed to Sun Wu and a separate, previously lost treatise attributed to Sun Bin, a later strategist and supposed descendant. The find confirms that a text bearing Sun Wu's name existed by the early Han dynasty, well before Sima Qian wrote, but it does not settle whether the biography Sima Qian recorded describes a real individual or a legend that had already solidified by his time.

What is not in dispute is the work's influence. Whoever assembled it, the Art of War became one of the most continuously studied strategic texts in world history, shaping Chinese military thought for two and a half millennia and, since the 20th century, business, sports, and negotiation strategy far beyond its original context.

whoThisIsFor: Anyone navigating sustained competition — in business, negotiation, or any high-stakes rivalry — who wants a framework built on positioning and information rather than direct confrontation.
whenToReadThis: Read before entering a competitive or adversarial situation where preparation and timing will matter more than raw effort in the moment.
sourceNotes:
v2 retrofit of a classical military text (compiled/attributed roughly 5th century BCE, traditionally to Sun Wu of Wu). Chapter structure and titles were verified against a full, direct reading of Lionel Giles' 1910 English translation (public domain), fetched and read in full during this session from sacred-texts.com (Chapters I-X, XII, and XIII read in their entirety, including Giles' scholarly footnotes and his own translator's introduction) and cross-checked against the table of contents on Wikisource and the MIT Internet Classics Archive. The v1 entry's 13-chapter list and titles (Laying Plans, Waging War, Attack by Stratagem, Tactical Dispositions, Energy, Weak Points and Strong, Maneuvering, Variation in Tactics, The Army on the March, Terrain, The Nine Situations, The Attack by Fire, The Use of Spies) were confirmed correct against Giles' real chapter list, with one small fix: Chapter VIII's actual Giles title is 'Variation of Tactics,' not 'Variation in Tactics' as v1 had it. Unlike most prior retrofits in this project, v1's structure here was largely accurate rather than invented.

All 30 quotes are exact wording drawn from Giles' 1910 translation, verified by direct reading of the primary source rather than recalled from memory or pulled from an internet 'Sun Tzu quotes' listicle — sourced from sacred-texts.com for Chapters I-X, XII, and XIII, and for the single Chapter XI quote (the shuai-jan/Wu-and-Yüeh passage), from Giles' own introduction, which quotes that exact passage from Ch. XI Sec. 30 verbatim while discussing the text's likely date of composition (the full body text of the long Ch. XI page could not be fetched in one pass this session; the quote used is Giles' verbatim translated wording of that passage, not a paraphrase). Deliberately excluded: the widely circulated internet line 'In the midst of chaos, there is also opportunity,' which appeared in the v1 entry's quote list but does not appear anywhere in Giles' translation and could not be traced to the actual text — a commonly garbled or invented 'internet Sun Tzu' line, dropped per this project's verification standard rather than retained on the strength of its popularity. Samuel B. Griffith's 1963 Oxford translation was consulted via secondary discussion (quoted at length in World History Encyclopedia's 'Sun-Tzu' article) but not used as a primary quote source; all 30 quotes here consistently follow Giles' wording and are labeled as such throughout, per the project's practice of picking one translation and noting it rather than mixing renderings.

authorBio addresses genuine, unresolved scholarly debate over Sun Tzu's historicity and authorship, drawn from direct reading (all fetched and read in full this session, not recalled from memory) of: (1) Lionel Giles' own 1910 introduction, which lays out at length his skepticism about the traditional Sima Qian biography, including calling the Ho Lu concubine-drill anecdote 'utterly preposterous and incredible,' and argues from internal textual evidence for a later date of composition; (2) World History Encyclopedia's 'Sun-Tzu' article (Joshua J. Mark, 2020); and (3) The 1440 Review's 'The Real Sun Tzu: Man, Myth or Legend?' (2023), which details the Zuo Zhuan's silence on Sun Wu, the anachronisms (crossbows, cavalry) pointing toward Warring States-era composition, and the 1972 Yinqueshan Han-tomb discovery of bamboo-strip texts under both Sun Wu's and Sun Bin's names. notableWorks was left empty deliberately — Sun Tzu is genuinely a one-text figure under any authorship theory, and inventing a broader bibliography would misrepresent that.
